item.title: Eat the Beans. Stop Selling Us the Apocalypse.
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos

item.content:encoded:
The promise of cheap insect protein skips an awkward expense: feeding the insects. Dressing that problem in futuristic packaging doesn’t make the economics work.

The apocalypse apparently comes with a product launch.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

First, we are told that familiar food will become unsustainable or unaffordable. Then comes the proposed adjustment: ordinary people will learn to eat insects. Somewhere between the warning and the investment pitch, an extraordinary assumption slips through unchallenged—that farming, feeding, harvesting, and processing another animal will provide a bargain replacement for the plants that animal eats.

A short video titled “That’s not how eating bugs works” cuts through that assumption with an admirably simple response: eat the beans.

It is a short video, not a scientific paper. Some of its claims need qualification. Its central economic objection deserves considerably more attention than the fantasy it punctures.

If your emergency food system begins by feeding edible crops to insects, you have added a production stage. You have not explained how hungry people get cheaper food.

The insects also need dinner

The seductive version of insect farming treats insects as a shortcut around agricultural constraints. Small creatures, small footprint, enormous promise. Protein arrives at the other end.

But a living organism is not a machine that manufactures nutrition from enthusiasm. It needs suitable feed. Raising it requires resources. Turning it into a shelf-stable product requires further work.

Those expenses need to buy something useful.

Researchers Mark Lundy and Michael Parrella examined that problem in a 2015 study with a title that should have survived every subsequent marketing presentation: Crickets Are Not a Free Lunch. Their experiments found that the quality of the feed substantially affected the results. Crickets raised on poultry feed offered little improvement in protein conversion over chickens; those given minimally processed municipal food waste suffered mortality above 99 percent. A processed food-waste diet performed better, producing harvestable insects with efficiencies similar to chickens.

That is a serious obstacle to the casual promise that insects will turn whatever we discard into abundant, cheap nourishment.

Feed them valuable agricultural inputs, and they compete for those inputs. Feed them unsuitable waste, and the system can fail. Process the waste into something suitable, and the processing becomes part of the bill.

The word “waste” does not make collection, preparation, transport, or quality control free.

A useful niche cannot carry a civilization-sized promise

There are legitimate possibilities here. Pretending otherwise would weaken the argument.

Research published in 2026 followed farmed crickets across five generations on diets incorporating spent grain. It found that high inclusion of that byproduct could support consistent performance across generations, although growth was affected. That is evidence worth investigating for particular production systems.

It does not establish that insect protein can undercut beans as a staple for people facing poverty.

These are different claims with different burdens of proof. Successfully raising an insect on an agricultural byproduct establishes a biological possibility. Establishing an affordable food system requires accounting for the entire operation, including the availability and competing uses of the feedstock, the facilities, labor, processing, and delivery.

A viable operation in one location does not establish a universal answer to hunger. A promising feed ingredient does not establish the cheapest human dinner. A successful experiment does not settle the retail price.

Apocalypse apologists want to jump from “this can be done” to “this is what ordinary people must learn to accept.” The missing steps are where the economics live.

Put beans in the comparison

Any proposal sold as an affordable answer to food scarcity should have to compete against ordinary plant foods.

That comparison is less glamorous than a futuristic protein facility. It is also unavoidable.

When humans can eat the crops being used as feed, the proposal needs to explain what justifies sending those crops through another animal first. Perhaps the resulting product offers qualities some customers value. Perhaps a particular operation uses inputs people cannot eat. Those are arguments to demonstrate, with actual costs attached.

They cannot simply be assumed.

Nor is it enough to announce that costs will fall with investment and scale. That is a forecast. The investment has a cost, the facilities have operating expenses, and the promised efficiencies have to materialize.

Even a substantial improvement would leave the relevant question intact: cheaper than what?

Cheaper than today’s specialty insect powder would be an achievement for its producer. Cheaper than an existing staple is a much more demanding claim.

Beans do not need a speculative future price to appear in that comparison. They are already food.

Disgust is a distraction

The argument does not require pretending that eating insects is degrading.

People have eaten insects across generations and cultures. Edible insects can provide protein and micronutrients. Treating those foods as inherently disgusting substitutes a cultural reflex for an economic argument.

Someone choosing insects because they enjoy them presents no political scandal. Someone developing a useful way to recover nutrients from a suitable byproduct may be doing worthwhile work.

The objection concerns the much larger sales pitch: that mass deprivation can be made manageable through a supposedly inevitable dietary adjustment whose affordability remains to be demonstrated.

Criticizing that pitch also requires no conspiracy about a secret plan to confiscate everyone’s dinner. The publicly available argument is weak enough on its own.

Show the inputs. Show the costs. Show the comparison with the staple foods people can already eat.

Futuristic packaging is not an exemption from arithmetic.

Scarcity is a convenient alibi

There is a political convenience in describing hunger primarily as a problem awaiting a new protein product.

It directs attention toward what people should learn to consume. Questions about what they can afford, who controls access, and which investments would actually improve their lives become supporting details in somebody else’s innovation story.

The public gets a lesson in adaptation. The entrepreneur gets a market.

An investor may see a commercial opportunity in an expensive product. A government may subsidize an industry. Neither decision establishes that the product is the least expensive way to feed people.

Coercion would not fix that arithmetic either. Authorities can impose inefficient systems, and favored suppliers can profit from them. But that would demonstrate the power to impose a costly arrangement—not prove the original claim that insects were the economical necessity.

This distinction matters because the language of inevitability excuses decisions before anyone has accounted for them. Once a future is presented as unavoidable, the people expected to endure it are invited to discuss their attitude rather than its terms.

They are allowed to be squeamish or adventurous. They are less welcome to demand the spreadsheet.

Dinner needs an argument that adds up

The short video does not prove that every insect farm will fail. It does not need to.

Its strongest point is that the cheap-protein promise contains a hungry middleman. Anyone proposing that middleman as an answer to mass food insecurity must demonstrate why the additional work produces a better result than feeding people suitable plant foods directly.

Specific insect-farming systems may earn their place. The sweeping promise has to earn its credibility.

Until then, “eat the beans” is a perfectly serious response to an industry-shaped answer that has skipped the comparison most likely to embarrass it.

People facing hunger deserve affordable food now. They do not owe anyone a market for an apocalypse product.

item.title: Stop having imposter syndrome!
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Before you decide you are unqualified, take a good look at the people who apparently are. You are hesitating over a job application because you meet eight of the ten requirements. Somewhere, a man whose casinos went bankrupt is running the United States. Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself: ☕ Buy us a coffee Perhaps you should submit the application. item.content:encoded:
Before you decide you are unqualified, take a good look at the people who apparently are.

You are hesitating over a job application because you meet eight of the ten requirements. Somewhere, a man whose casinos went bankrupt is running the United States.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Perhaps you should submit the application.

Donald Trump built a political identity around his supposed business genius. His record includes the Trump Taj Mahal entering Chapter 11 in 1991, followed by Trump’s Castle and the Trump Plaza casino in 1992. His casino and resort companies returned to bankruptcy proceedings in 2004 and 2009. These were corporate reorganizations, with creditors and ownership stakes on the line, under the name of the man selling himself as the master of the deal.

A casino’s central proposition is that the odds favor the house. Trump managed to make the house need protection from its creditors.

And you are worried somebody will discover you needed help with a spreadsheet.

There comes a point when the visible quality of leadership should force a reassessment of the standards you impose on yourself. We have not reached that point. We have passed it. A long time ago. The people at the top have supplied the supporting documentation.

Trump sold business genius through repeated failure

A casino can fail. Debt, competition, and bad economic conditions can overwhelm a gambling business. But the man who demands credit for his brilliance also owns his decisions about borrowing, expansion, and management. Trump’s repeated casino troubles belong in the assessment of the expertise he sold.

His name did not turn financial failure into modesty. The failures became material for another explanation of why he was exceptionally clever.

Consider what that does to the story you tell yourself. You make an error and wonder whether your entire career rests on a misunderstanding. Trump’s businesses went through repeated bankruptcy proceedings, and he continued marketing his name as a certificate of exceptional judgment.

The business instruction carried its own grim punch line. In 2016, he agreed to a $25 million settlement resolving litigation over alleged fraud at Trump University, without admitting wrongdoing. The venture that sold access to his business wisdom ended up funding compensation for customers who challenged what they had been sold.

His charitable foundation supplied a different kind of disgrace. It shut down amid litigation over misconduct, and Trump paid $2 million in court-ordered damages for misuse of charitable funds.

Financial failure and abuse are different failings. Neither belongs on a résumé offered as proof that everyone else should defer to your superior judgment.

Yet the name stayed on the product. The authority kept expanding. The audience was repeatedly asked to admire the salesman rather than examine the returns.

You are allowed to examine the returns.

The ignorance survived the promotion

The presidency gave Trump a platform on which the gap between confidence and understanding became impossible to miss.

At an April 2020 coronavirus briefing, after hearing about disinfectants killing the virus on surfaces, he publicly wondered whether something similar could be done inside the body, including “by injection inside or almost a cleaning.”

This was the president of the United States, during a public health emergency, treating an elementary distinction between disinfecting a surface and treating a patient as an opportunity for presidential brainstorming.

You worry about asking a basic question in a meeting. He workshopped internal disinfectant from the White House podium.

The public evidence of incompetence did not stop with him. In March 2025, senior administration officials discussed impending strikes in Yemen in a Signal group that accidentally included Jeffrey Goldberg, editor in chief of The Atlantic. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth shared operational details. Reporting then revealed another chat in which he shared attack details with participants including his wife, brother, and personal lawyer. Trump defended him in April.

Most office workers understand that checking the recipients matters before sending sensitive information. These men had military operations to discuss.

Remember that the next time you interpret a moment of uncertainty as evidence that you are fundamentally unsuited to responsibility.

There is also a danger in attributing every destructive act to stupidity. Authoritarian cruelty can be deliberate. A government can understand precisely whom it is hurting and proceed enthusiastically. Deliberate abuse requires exposure and resistance; incompetence adds another reason to reject the presumption that power deserves intellectual deference.

A title cannot supply the judgment its holder lacks. Neither can a flag behind a podium.

Corporate leaders offer the same lesson

The private sector has supplied plenty of material for dismantling your inferiority complex.

In November 2022, Mark Zuckerberg acknowledged misreading the durability of the pandemic’s online commerce boom and increasing investment on that basis. In the message admitting the mistake, he announced that more than 11,000 Meta employees would lose their jobs. A few months later, he announced plans for roughly another 10,000 job cuts.

He got the forecast wrong. Other people got the career interruption.

That record does not mean Zuckerberg has never made a successful decision. It means the mythology of the executive who operates on a plane of understanding inaccessible to ordinary people deserves to be dragged down to earth.

At Warner Bros. Discovery, David Zaslav’s reported compensation rose to $51.9 million for 2024, including approximately $23.9 million in cash incentive compensation. In the same year, the company reported an $11.3 billion net loss attributable to WBD, including a large noncash goodwill impairment. It also generated positive free cash flow, a measure the board used in rewarding him.

Executive performance comes with people whose job is to explain the context, select the relevant measures, and establish why the reward remains deserved.

Your inner critic will prosecute you over an awkward sentence in an email.

At least give yourself the courtesy of considering the evidence in your favor.

Stop giving their confidence more weight than your work

The most corrosive part of impostor thinking is the assumption that everyone else passed a test you somehow evaded.

You imagine that the confident people understand everything you struggle with. You interpret their certainty as knowledge and your questions as deficiency. You see your own preparation, revisions, and uncertainty from the inside, then compare them with somebody else’s finished performance of authority.

Look at what powerful people have actually done. Confidence survives ignorance with remarkable ease. It can survive repeated failure. It can even recruit an audience to defend the failure.

That should change how much authority you grant the voice telling you that uncertainty means you do not belong.

Knowing that you need to check a figure is useful judgment. Recognizing the limits of your knowledge gives you a reason to investigate. Correcting yourself can improve the work. Those habits deserve credit in your assessment of your competence.

Self-doubt does not establish that you are qualified. Neither does its absence establish that they are. Your ability deserves to be judged through the work you can do, the preparation you bring, and your willingness to learn.

Keep your standards. Make them proportionate. Stop demanding omniscience as the admission price for your own participation while treating a powerful person’s confidence as sufficient evidence of theirs.

Apply for the position. Put your name on the work. Make the argument you can support. Learn what you need to learn, and correct what you get wrong.

Donald Trump’s casinos needed bankruptcy protection. His administration managed to include a journalist in a conversation about impending military strikes. Corporate leaders have admitted expensive mistakes and remained empowered to decide whose job disappears.

You do not need to imitate their recklessness to stop being intimidated by their authority.

Before you decide you are the impostor, look up.

item.title: Who Gets to Fail Without Losing Their Legitimacy
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Workers are told to prove they deserve their jobs. Powerful executives can make disastrous decisions and retain the authority to decide whose job disappears. item.content:encoded:
Workers are told to prove they deserve their jobs. Powerful executives can make disastrous decisions and retain the authority to decide whose job disappears.

Mark Zuckerberg got the forecast wrong. More than 11,000 other people lost their jobs.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

In November 2022, Zuckerberg acknowledged that he had mistaken the pandemic surge in online commerce for a lasting transformation and increased investment accordingly. In the same message, he announced mass layoffs.

“I got this wrong, and I take responsibility for that,” he wrote.

The admission was his. The termination notices went elsewhere.

That sequence exposes a double standard beneath corporate sermons about accountability. The people who approve consequential mistakes can retain the authority to explain them, define the recovery, and decide who must sacrifice. Employees who never approved the strategy can lose their livelihoods implementing its correction.

Power includes the privilege of surviving your own judgment. For workers, even somebody else’s bad judgment can be enough to end a career chapter.

Executives retain authority while workers lose employment

Zuckerberg’s message acknowledged several pressures, including competition, economic conditions, and changes affecting advertising. Meta offered departing American employees at least 16 weeks of base pay, additional pay for tenure, and six months of healthcare coverage. Those protections mattered to the people receiving them. The decision still removed their employment while leaving its author in command.

In March 2023, Zuckerberg announced plans to eliminate roughly another 10,000 jobs and close approximately 5,000 unfilled positions. The organizing slogan was the “Year of Efficiency.” The executive who had acknowledged misreading the business environment remained empowered to decide what efficiency required.

Corporate language makes this arrangement sound almost tender. Leaders announce difficult decisions. They express gratitude. They praise colleagues whose departure they have authorized. The compassion resides in the message; the coercion resides in who gets to send it.

An admission of error can become another demonstration of leadership, another opportunity to perform seriousness before an audience. For the employee, the corresponding event is the loss of income and a search for work.

At Meta, Zuckerberg’s authority has a concrete foundation. Its 2026 proxy statement identifies the company as controlled because he holds a majority of its outstanding voting power. Meta voluntarily maintains a majority-independent board, but the concentration of voting control remains.

The founder’s position is secured by ownership. The employee’s position lasts until management decides it no longer serves the plan.

Telling both people to develop more confidence is an absurd response to the difference between them.

Boards decide which results deserve rewards

David Zaslav’s compensation at Warner Bros. Discovery illustrates another mechanism that protects executive standing: the power to evaluate success through a carefully selected set of measures.

For 2024, WBD reported $39.3 billion in revenue, down 4% excluding currency effects, and an $11.3 billion net loss attributable to the company. That loss included a $9.1 billion noncash goodwill impairment in its television networks business. WBD also generated $4.4 billion in free cash flow.

Zaslav’s reported compensation rose from $49.7 million in 2023 to $51.9 million in 2024. The latter included stock awards valued at their grant date and approximately $23.9 million in cash incentive compensation. The board tied rewards to measures including free cash flow and strategic objectives; certain CEO share awards earned payouts at 200% of target.

An executive’s performance receives a framework sophisticated enough to distinguish among outcomes, recognize favorable indicators, and explain why substantial rewards remain appropriate.

Employees need that same attention to context. Their work can be competent and valuable while the strategy above them fails. A department can meet its obligations and still be eliminated. A person can do everything management requested and discover that management’s next request is their departure.

The board’s willingness to recognize complexity at the top makes the bluntness imposed below especially offensive. Senior leadership receives an account of the achievements that justify its compensation. Workers receive an account of the pressures that justify their removal.

The asymmetry reaches beyond annual pay. In March 2026, Reuters reported that Zaslav could receive a package of up to $887 million associated with the proposed Paramount Skydance transaction, including severance, equity, and a tax reimbursement whose value depended on timing. Even as a conditional estimate, the arrangement reveals the scale of protection available through an executive contract.

For people at that level, departure itself can be an event worth hundreds of millions. For the workforce, departure means calculating how long severance will cover the bills.

Workers bear lasting costs for decisions they did not make

Job loss reaches far beyond the day someone packs a desk.

Research summarized by the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago examined workers aged 25 to 55 who were displaced between 1989 and 2019 after at least two years of full-time employment with their employer. Ten years after displacement, their earnings remained approximately 25% below those of workers who had not been displaced. The researchers attributed the persistent effect primarily to lower-paying subsequent employment.

The research concerns involuntary job loss for reasons other than individual performance. Its significance is brutal: workers can suffer lasting financial damage without having failed at their jobs.

That destroys the comforting fiction that employment insecurity simply rewards effort and punishes incompetence. Performance cannot reliably protect a person from decisions they have no authority to prevent.

Meanwhile, the survival of powerful executives is routinely available to be mistaken for evidence of their superior judgment. They remain in the chair, so they must deserve the chair. The employees disappear, so their disappearance must have been necessary.

The reasoning grants authority the power to certify itself.

A business can benefit financially from layoffs while the displaced workers suffer. Investors can approve the recovery while families absorb its costs. Those outcomes can coexist because a company’s financial measures do not capture everyone who pays for its decisions.

A rising share price cannot retroactively make a worker responsible for the strategy that eliminated their job.

Accountability must follow decision making power

Organizations need room to experiment, make mistakes, and learn. The people doing their work need security through that process.

Instead, corporate hierarchy can grant patience to a leader’s vision while demanding immediate sacrifice from the workforce. Executives invoke the uncertainty of business to explain disappointing results, then invoke the necessity of business to explain layoffs. Their authority survives both explanations.

This arrangement is maintained through ownership structures, contracts, compensation rules, and unequal bargaining power. It will survive any number of motivational speeches about believing in yourself.

Changing it requires workers to have more power over the decisions that govern their lives: stronger collective bargaining rights, meaningful representation in corporate governance, enforceable notice and severance protections, and compensation rules that make senior leaders bear more of the downside of strategies they authorize.

Boards should assess workforce harm alongside the financial measures they reward. Leaders claiming credit for an organization’s achievements should face consequences proportionate to their control when their decisions damage it.

Workers already live with consequences. They adapt to reorganizations, compete for replacement jobs, and absorb interruptions to their earnings. What they lack is an equivalent say in the choices producing those consequences.

The executive’s mistake becomes a lesson. The worker’s lost job becomes a gap to explain.

That is the privilege at the center of corporate legitimacy: the right to keep deciding after other people have paid for your decisions.

item.title: 'Turn around sir!' Judge gives DOJ lawyer a courtroom reality check
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: A federal judge told Justice Department lawyer Adam R.F. Gustafson to turn around after he claimed ignorance of public opposition to the Trump administration’s East Potomac Park golf-course plan. Hundreds of people in the courtroom raised their hands, according to Lawfare reporter Molly Roberts. The exchange was more than a lawyer losing an argument with the room: It exposed the government’s broader strategy of treating a documented plan as somehow unknowable whenever a direct answer might carry
item.content:encoded:
A federal judge told Justice Department lawyer Adam R.F. Gustafson to turn around after he claimed ignorance of public opposition to the Trump administration’s East Potomac Park golf-course plan. Hundreds of people in the courtroom raised their hands, according to Lawfare reporter Molly Roberts. The exchange was more than a lawyer losing an argument with the room: It exposed the government’s broader strategy of treating a documented plan as somehow unknowable whenever a direct answer might carry legal or political consequences.

A design everyone could see but no one would own

At Friday’s hearing, Judge Ana Reyes pressed Gustafson and Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward about the proposed redesign of the course. Interior had submitted a design to the National Capital Planning Commission. The Commission of Fine Arts was considering the same design. President Donald Trump had posted it on Truth Social.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Still, Woodward would not identify it as the final plan. The government’s position was that additional steps and approvals remained, making a definitive answer premature. Reyes stripped away that procedural fog and asked a narrower question: Assuming the necessary approvals are obtained, is the Tom Fazio “championship-style” course the administration intends to build?

Gustafson finally said it was the current plan.

That distinction matters. Reyes was not asking whether every approval had already been secured or whether construction was complete. She was asking what the administration was pursuing. The Justice Department repeatedly answered the question it preferred—a lawyerly lecture about contingencies—until the judge forced it to address the one she actually posed.

When Gustafson asked her to repeat herself, Reyes told him it would “behoove” him to listen. The irritation was earned. Evasion does not become candor merely because officials phrase it as uncertainty.

The public was directly behind him

Reyes then asked whether the plan had encountered pushback. Gustafson replied that he had not “polled the public,” prompting the judge to say it would have been ridiculous for her to ask whether he had. She instructed him to listen to her questions and assume she was not asking “an idiotic question.”

Gustafson said his knowledge was largely confined to what had happened in court. He added that he did not have a television and therefore did not know what people thought about the golf course.

Reyes supplied an immediate, if informal, demonstration. She asked those in the courtroom with strong feelings about the project to raise their hands, then told Gustafson: “Turn around, sir.” Roberts reported that hundreds of arms went up, representing most of the room.

The display was not a scientific measure of District opinion, and Reyes did not present it as one. It did, however, demolish Gustafson’s performance of institutional isolation. A senior government lawyer had reduced public opposition to information he supposedly could not access because he did not watch television, while a courtroom full of concerned people sat directly behind him.

The credibility dispute is now part of the case

The golf-course design is only one front in a deeper dispute over whether the administration and its lawyers have been truthful with the court. According to AlterNet, the hearing followed a whistleblower’s disclosure that the administration was destroying documents containing conversations about presidential construction projects in Washington.

Reyes has appointed a special master to investigate whether the Justice Department misled the court about events in the case. The department filed its opposition to that appointment on Thursday. Reyes has also begun hearings by asking whether anyone needs to correct an inadvertently false statement previously made to the court.

On Friday, she made the stakes explicit. After asking whether those present knew the meaning of a “zeptosecond”—an extraordinarily brief unit of time—Reyes said that if she learned documents had been destroyed, she would begin sanctions or contempt proceedings “in a zeptosecond.”

That warning does not establish that records were destroyed or that Justice Department lawyers lied. Those are the questions under examination. But the appointment of a special master and Reyes’s repeated invitations to correct the record show that the court’s concern is no longer confined to the merits of a landscaping proposal. The government’s credibility has itself become an issue requiring supervision.

The administration has the institutional machinery to propose the redevelopment, submit its preferred design and defend the project in federal court. The public has raised hands. Reyes’s questions cut through that imbalance by requiring the officials exercising power to identify what they are doing. On Friday, even that elementary demand for a straight answer produced a fight.

item.content:encoded:
Ava DuVernay postponed the release of 14th, her documentary about the constitutional fight over birthright citizenship and equal protection, after Stacey Abrams advised her that the film would be more useful after the 2026 midterm elections. The decision moved its global Netflix debut to December 4, with limited U.S. and U.K. theatrical screenings beginning November 27.

That is the substance behind the suggestion that Abrams wanted a “potentially explosive” film kept under wraps. Nothing in AlterNet’s report indicates that she sought to suppress the documentary, feared its contents, or considered it politically damaging. DuVernay described a strategic disagreement over timing: she wanted the film released before the election; Abrams argued that the political forces examined in it would remain after the ballots were counted.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A delay, not a disappearance

“It was Stacey Abrams who said to me, ‘You shouldn’t do that,’” DuVernay said Thursday at The Washington Post’s Global Women’s Summit. According to DuVernay, the former Georgia gubernatorial candidate and voting-rights advocate believed 14th would be “more needed and more instructive after” the midterms.

DuVernay accepted that advice. Her account gives Abrams substantial influence over the release schedule, but not control over the film itself. The documentary is still receiving a theatrical and Netflix release, and the report identifies no demand from Abrams to alter its arguments or remove material.

Calling the film “potentially explosive” supplies intrigue that the reported facts do not. The actual political calculation is more revealing: Abrams expected the conflict surrounding the Fourteenth Amendment to survive the election, regardless of its outcome.

“What she really was saying to me is that the opposition is not going away,” DuVernay told the Post’s Geoff Edgers. “These ideas are not going away, the money behind it is not going away, and it will come back with a vengeance.”

That assessment treats elections as episodes in a longer struggle rather than as clean resolutions. It also points toward the durable machinery behind constitutional reaction: organized ideas, sustained financing and institutions capable of carrying an agenda forward after one campaign ends.

The constitutional terrain

DuVernay’s first documentary in a decade examines more than 150 years of conflict over the Fourteenth Amendment. Ratified in 1868 after the Civil War, the amendment establishes birthright citizenship and requires states to provide equal protection under the law.

Those guarantees are not historical decoration. They determine who belongs to the political community and who may demand protection from government power. A fight over the amendment is therefore a fight over the state’s authority to define citizenship and distribute legal rights.

Abrams’s advice, as DuVernay recounted it, rested on the expectation that the forces challenging those principles would retain money and momentum after Election Day. The film’s delayed release reflects that judgment. Whether postponement makes the documentary more instructive or merely removes it from a moment when it could have shaped public debate cannot be established from the report. DuVernay made the choice, and the political cost of that choice is straightforward: voters will not see the film before casting their midterm ballots.

Fear converted into a film

DuVernay told The Guardian that conditions under President Donald Trump drove her work on the documentary. She described people in Los Angeles being pulled from cars, a flower seller near her office abruptly disappearing and people she knows hiding inside their homes.

“It’s been a very tough two years,” she said. When she felt “the rage and the fear,” she put those emotions into the film: “I was doing something.”

These are DuVernay’s observations and characterization, not findings independently established in AlterNet’s account. But they explain why she regarded the project as urgent. For her, the Fourteenth Amendment is connected to people’s immediate vulnerability to state power, not confined to a classroom dispute over constitutional language.

14th also extends the work of her 2016 documentary 13th, which examined race, mass incarceration and the Thirteenth Amendment’s exception permitting involuntary servitude as punishment for crime. The titles locate both films in the gap between constitutional promises and the systems built around their exceptions, contested meanings and uneven enforcement.

Abrams did not bury that argument. She persuaded DuVernay to hold it until after the election because, in her view, the political operation confronting those guarantees would still be there. The film’s release schedule now embodies that wager—and leaves the public to judge whether waiting strengthened the intervention or surrendered the moment when it might have mattered most.

item.title: Disbarred MAGA lawyer claims far-right Florida court caved to the left
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Florida’s Supreme Court suspended Larry Klayman from practicing law for two years after disciplinary findings involving conflicts of interest, client confidentiality and his refusal to withdraw from a case when his client fired him. Klayman’s answer was not to confront those findings. He blamed a “highly politicized” appellate court, invoked alleged left-wing bias and threatened to sue the journalist reporting his response. item.content:encoded:
Florida’s Supreme Court suspended Larry Klayman from practicing law for two years after disciplinary findings involving conflicts of interest, client confidentiality and his refusal to withdraw from a case when his client fired him. Klayman’s answer was not to confront those findings. He blamed a “highly politicized” appellate court, invoked alleged left-wing bias and threatened to sue the journalist reporting his response.

That defense turns an attorney-discipline case into a familiar MAGA grievance: professional consequences become political persecution, even when the institution imposing them is controlled entirely by Republican appointees.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The conduct behind the suspension

The Florida action followed Klayman’s earlier suspension in Washington over his representation of Elham Sataki, a Voice of America employee who retained him for a lawsuit against the broadcaster in 2009.

According to the disciplinary record described by the Florida Supreme Court, Klayman developed feelings for Sataki that compromised his representation. The court cited messages in which he told her that his emotions had left him unable to function as her lawyer.

The findings extended beyond an undisclosed emotional conflict. The court concluded that Klayman violated Sataki’s confidentiality and trust by publicizing her sexual-harassment case beyond what she wanted. After she asked him to stop representing her, he failed to withdraw, according to the filing reported by the Miami New Times.

The D.C. Court of Appeals had separately suspended Klayman for 90 days in 2020 after finding that he represented clients suing Judicial Watch without first securing the organization’s consent. Klayman, who founded and led the right-wing legal group, denied wrongdoing.

Florida’s disciplinary order followed those Washington proceedings. Although AlterNet at one point describes the unsigned order as disbarment, its report identifies the sanction as a two-year suspension. That distinction matters: a temporary suspension is not permanent expulsion from the profession.

A partisan story that avoids the disciplinary record

Klayman told the New Times that the punishment did not arise from his conduct but from a politicized appeals court working against Republicans. As supposed proof, he pointed to proceedings involving Rudy Giuliani, Republican senators Josh Hawley and Ted Cruz, and former Trump adviser Kellyanne Conway.

That argument does not answer the findings against him. Naming prominent conservatives who have faced professional scrutiny cannot establish that Klayman maintained his client’s confidence, avoided a conflict of interest or withdrew when dismissed. It merely replaces the substance of the case with partisan affiliation.

Klayman said he would seek reconsideration and pursue related litigation aimed at reversing the D.C. suspension, which he argued would undermine the Florida order. He complained that Florida’s order contained no factual or legal reasoning. But the underlying disciplinary history reported by the New Times is concrete: two separate matters, findings by the D.C. appellate court and reciprocal consequences in Florida.

His response to the reporter followed the same pattern of displacement. “Get this right or you and Miami New Times will be sued again!” he wrote. The threat did nothing to rebut the ethics findings. It instead placed pressure on the person describing them.

Republican appointees become “the left”

Klayman’s political explanation becomes especially strained at the Florida Supreme Court. As of January 2026, all seven justices had been appointed by Republican governors, including six selected by Gov. Ron DeSantis. The court is widely regarded as one of the country’s most conservative state supreme courts.

That does not automatically make every ruling correct or apolitical. It does make Klayman’s accusation revealing. In this grievance system, an institution does not remain conservative because of its composition, record or authority. It remains conservative only while producing the desired result. Once it imposes an adverse consequence, it can be recast as an instrument of the left.

The maneuver also redirects attention from the person with the least institutional power in the underlying case: the client whose wishes, confidentiality and decision to end the representation were allegedly disregarded. Klayman presents himself as the victim of courts and ideologues. The disciplinary findings describe a lawyer who would not respect his own client’s boundaries.

Florida’s Republican-appointed justices did not need to become liberals to suspend him. They needed only to treat professional rules as applying to a politically connected conservative lawyer. Klayman’s complaint rests on the increasingly explicit premise that doing so is itself partisan misconduct.

item.title: Dazed Fox News hosts struggle to decode ‘message’ to Trump
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos

item.content:encoded:
Fox News’ post-midterm bewilderment could not conceal the message its own polling had already delivered: voters were angry about the Iran war, economic pressure, affordability and corruption, and they punished Republicans accordingly. The mystery confronting the hosts of Fox & Friends was not what voters said. It was whether Donald Trump and the political operation built around him were willing to hear it.

AlterNet reported that Fox personalities reacted Friday to what the outlet described as a historic Republican defeat, including losses in reliably conservative states. Host Ainsley Earhardt called the results “shocking” and “mind-blowing,” while asking whether the country had succumbed to “Republican fatigue” or simply wanted change.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

That framing made voter judgment sound like an atmospheric condition afflicting the GOP. But the network’s own figures pointed to decisions, costs and governing failures—not an inexplicable exhaustion with a party label.

Fox had the answer before it found the question

Fox political anchor Bret Baier said Republicans faced powerful headwinds from the economy, gasoline prices and the war in Iran. “This country is not into this war,” he concluded. Fox’s data, he added, showed anger across several issues.

Lawrence Jones rejected even Baier’s cautious description. Voters in conservative states, he argued, were telling Republican leaders: “You’re not listening to me.” He noted that respondents told Fox pollsters they rejected socialism but still elected candidates he characterized as socialist. In Jones’ reading, those votes were not ideological conversions; they were an attempt to force the people in power to pay attention.

That interpretation is plausible, but it also preserves a comforting Republican assumption: voters who rejected GOP candidates must still fundamentally belong to the right. Their ballots become a temporary protest rather than a decision that Democratic candidates, whatever labels Fox applies to them, offered a preferable alternative.

Baier called the backlash the “red scream,” borrowing Republican strategist Alex Castellanos’ description. The phrase dramatizes the electorate’s anger while keeping the focus on its emotional volume. Yet voters were not merely screaming to be seen. According to Fox’s own analysis, they identified policies and conditions for which the governing party could be held responsible.

Laura Ingraham said 94 percent of midterm voters considered the Iran war a major factor in their vote. She stressed that the finding was “just a fact” and said subsequent polling showed the same pattern. Trey Gowdy argued that Trump’s political problem extended further, with affordability and corruption cited by even more voters.

The hosts’ confusion therefore had limits. Fox could measure the discontent, name its sources and warn the president about it. What the network struggled to process was the consequence: voters acted on that anger even when doing so meant electing candidates whom conservative media had told them to fear.

Texas punctured the mythology of popularity

Earhardt treated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott’s reported loss in Texas as especially difficult to reconcile. “Everyone loves him in Texas,” she said, contrasting Abbott with Ken Paxton, whose “controversial past” she acknowledged had made him a less universally appealing candidate.

But an incumbent losing by more than a percentage point is direct evidence against the claim that everyone loves him. Earhardt’s formulation placed Republican popularity beyond dispute and turned the actual vote into the anomaly. That is not analysis so much as insulation: the politician remains beloved, while the electorate somehow produces the wrong result.

Calling the outcome “Republican fatigue” performs similar work. Fatigue suggests that voters grew bored with a successful product. The explanations cited elsewhere on Fox were far more concrete. People faced affordability problems, resented corruption and opposed a war. If those issues drove the result, Republicans were not defeated by mere overexposure. They were judged for what government did under their control.

Advice from an apparatus built around Trump

Fox’s reckoning also exposed the network’s institutional position. Its personalities were not detached observers trying to understand an unfamiliar administration. AlterNet described Fox as aligned with Trump, and several hosts used their programs to offer him direct political advice.

Ingraham urged Trump to “do some hard thinking” about voters’ priorities and to “move on” from the Iran war. Veteran Republican strategist Karl Rove said Trump appeared to believe he was still winning and called on the party to abandon his “performance art” politics. Conservative radio host Erick Erickson likewise argued that Trump’s persistently “crazy” conduct meant Republicans should move beyond MAGA.

Those interventions matter because conservative media did not merely report Trump’s dominance of the Republican Party. It helped sustain the political environment in which loyalty to him became a governing strategy and dissent became suspect. After the losses, some of the same voices were attempting to reposition themselves as messengers carrying public discontent upward to the leader.

Their concern, according to AlterNet, was that Trump was doubling down on the policies and conduct they believed had cost Republicans the midterms. Rove’s observation captured the underlying problem: a political movement organized around its leader’s self-image has few internal mechanisms for correction when that image collides with electoral reality.

Fox’s polling had already decoded the message. Voters associated Republican power with an unpopular war, economic pain and corruption, then used the means available to them to impose a consequence. The remaining uncertainty was not what they meant. It was whether Trump’s allies would treat the verdict as a demand for different government—or merely as a communications problem to manage until the next election.

item.title: Judge rebukes DOJ after lawyer accuses her of asking 'unserious questions'
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos

item.content:encoded:
The Justice Department conceded that President Donald Trump’s public demand helped determine when the federal government would close a Washington, D.C., golf course he wants renovated—after first portraying the matching date as coincidence. The admission came during a contentious hearing in which Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General Adam R.F. Gustafson dismissed one of U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes’s questions as potentially unserious, earning an immediate rebuke.

The exchange mattered for more than courtroom etiquette. Reyes was testing whether the administration had manufactured the conditions it now cited to justify urgent action, then wrapped a presidential directive in the language of public safety.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A presidential deadline becomes an official decision

Trump posted on Truth Social that the course had to close on Nov. 15. The government subsequently selected Nov. 15, while Gustafson initially maintained that the alignment was coincidental.

According to AlterNet’s account of live reporting by Lawfare’s Molly Roberts, the Justice Department eventually identified three connected considerations behind the date: alleged safety hazards, the impending absence of a course operator, and Trump’s statement calling for closure that day.

That concession stripped away the most convenient version of the government’s story. The date was not simply the neutral product of an administrative safety review. By the department’s own account, the president’s pronouncement was one of the factors shaping the decision.

The administration offered two principal justifications for shutting the course: the property was dangerous to the public, and nobody would remain to manage it because the government had terminated the operator’s contract. Reyes focused on the circularity of the second argument. The administration created the management problem and then invoked that problem as a reason for closure.

Her analogy was blunt: a person cannot set their own house on fire and then claim entitlement to the insurance proceeds. Gustafson said the situation was more complicated, but complexity does not erase agency. If the government ends a contract and thereby removes the operator, it cannot honestly present the resulting vacancy as an external emergency that simply befell it.

The safety emergency arrived late

The department’s safety rationale drew similar scrutiny. It argued that conditions around the island and its seawall posed risks, including the possibility that children could be injured. Yet, as Reyes noted, roughly 30,000 people had recently come through the area for a marathon.

That did not establish that the property was safe. It did expose a basic inconsistency in the government’s claimed urgency: officials allowed a mass public event near the alleged hazard, had identified concerns months earlier, and still waited until Trump announced a Nov. 15 closure to treat those concerns as grounds for emergency action.

Gustafson compared the situation to unsafe roads that governments improve as money becomes available. Reyes tested that logic with a hypothetical about a government building at risk of collapsing and killing somebody. Would officials leave such a building open despite the danger?

“Your Honor, I’m not sure that’s a serious question,” Gustafson replied.

“You can be assured it’s a serious question because I asked it, and I don’t ask unserious questions,” Reyes answered.

The rebuke was deserved, but the underlying exchange was more revealing than the discourtesy. Reyes was asking the Justice Department to define the risk standard it wanted the court to accept. Gustafson responded by questioning the legitimacy of the inquiry instead of resolving the contradiction.

When Reyes asked whether officials ordinarily address critical hazards in places used by thousands of people, the department answered that they do so “gradually.” She then observed that nothing had been addressed since May, when the case reportedly did not feature claims of imminent danger. The government’s position therefore depended on two descriptions at once: the hazards were serious enough to require a sudden closure, but not serious enough to prompt remedial work over the preceding months.

The court refused the administration’s preferred framing

The administration holds the relevant executive power here. It terminated the management contract, advanced the safety justification, selected the closure date and defended those choices in court. Trump supplied the public deadline. Treating the outcome as bureaucratic happenstance would obscure the chain of responsibility Reyes forced the government to acknowledge.

The available reporting does not establish that the safety concerns themselves are fabricated. It does show that the Justice Department struggled to explain why those concerns became urgent only when they aligned with Trump’s renovation plans and stated deadline. That is the central issue: not whether hazards can exist, but whether officials are using them consistently or opportunistically.

By the lunch break, the government had moved from insisting on coincidence to admitting that Trump’s Nov. 15 declaration helped determine the Nov. 15 closure. Reyes’s questions did not create that contradiction. They prevented the Justice Department from talking around it.

item.title: Ex-prosecutor calls golf course proceedings 'utterly intolerable'
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Former federal prosecutor Joyce Vance called the position of Justice Department lawyers defending the Trump administration’s handling of East Potomac Park “utterly intolerable”: President Donald Trump was publicly intervening while the government’s credibility with U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes deteriorated over plans affecting the park’s golf course. item.content:encoded:
Former federal prosecutor Joyce Vance called the position of Justice Department lawyers defending the Trump administration’s handling of East Potomac Park “utterly intolerable”: President Donald Trump was publicly intervening while the government’s credibility with U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes deteriorated over plans affecting the park’s golf course. What should have been a routine land-use dispute had become a test of whether federal attorneys could still expect judicial trust after the administration cut down more than 400 trees and plaintiffs accused it of preparing further changes under cover of a temporary closure.

The immediate question before Reyes was whether to block a park shutdown scheduled to begin Sunday, Nov. 15. According to Vance, the plaintiffs argued that the closure was a prelude to restructuring the golf course and changing its landscaping in ways that would affect local use. The deeper dispute was whether the administration had dealt honestly with the court about plans it had pursued during the preceding year.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The government spent its presumption of good faith

Vance told MS NOW host Alicia Menendez that Reyes initially gave the Justice Department the customary presumption of regularity. The judge, she said, assumed government lawyers were speaking truthfully and making representations in good faith.

That deference did not survive the administration’s conduct. AlterNet reports that the removal of more than 400 trees marked a turning point, after which Reyes stopped giving Justice Department lawyers the benefit of the doubt. Vance described the judge’s posture as a practical application of “fool me once, shame on you; fool me twice, shame on me.”

That is not a minor courtroom embarrassment. The Justice Department enters federal court backed by institutional credibility accumulated over decades. When an administration exhausts that credibility, its lawyers lose more than a tactical advantage: judges begin scrutinizing assurances that would ordinarily carry substantial weight. The administration holds the land, commands the executive agencies and employs the attorneys defending its actions. The plaintiffs’ limited protection is the court’s ability to stop an irreversible project before the government makes litigation pointless by altering the property first.

Vance said the plaintiffs had strong evidence supporting both their request for an injunction and their likelihood of prevailing on the merits because “the government is not playing by the rules.” That was her legal assessment, not a ruling reported in the supplied account. Reyes was still pressing the government on whether it had made a final decision to implement the new park plans.

Trump made his lawyers defend his interference

Menendez asked how difficult it was for government attorneys to work while the president was “fundamentally undermining them at every turn.” Vance’s answer stripped away the occupational sympathy: in private practice, a lawyer whose client behaved this way could fire the client. A Justice Department attorney could withdraw from the case or resign.

“The first time that your client does that to you, you fire the client, or if you’re a Justice Department attorney, you take yourself off of the case or you resign because it’s utterly intolerable,” Vance said.

Trump had inserted himself into the dispute through posts on Truth Social, according to the report. That intervention matters because Justice Department lawyers do not represent Trump’s personal tastes. They represent the United States. Yet they were left asking a federal judge to trust an administration whose most powerful official was publicly involving himself in a contested project while the court examined whether its plans had been disclosed honestly.

The resulting dysfunction should not be miscast as hapless attorneys struggling with a difficult client. Trump is not an unruly outsider to the executive branch; he controls it. The lawyers appearing before Reyes operate beneath the president’s authority, and their professional predicament follows from decisions made at the top. They may face uncomfortable choices, as Vance argued, but the government’s credibility problem belongs to the administration they represent.

A public park caught in a program of presidential vanity

Vance placed the golf-course dispute alongside Trump’s other projects in Washington, including his interventions involving the Kennedy Center and his proposed giant arch. The common feature is the use of federal power and public space to pursue the president’s preferred aesthetic and commemorative projects.

Calling these “vanity projects” is an interpretation, but the power imbalance is concrete. Local users do not control East Potomac Park. The executive branch does. If the plaintiffs are correct that the announced closure would allow the administration to begin tearing up the course and imposing a new layout before the legal dispute is resolved, the shutdown would not be an administrative footnote. It would give the government the opportunity to create facts on the ground while insisting in court that no final decision had been made.

That is the misdirection at the center of the case. The controversy is not principally about whether government lawyers have an unpleasant assignment, nor merely about landscaping preferences. It is about whether an administration can preserve strategic ambiguity in court while retaining the practical ability to transform public property. Reyes’s skepticism reflects the consequence of that approach: once the government persuades a judge that its assurances cannot safely be trusted, even an ostensibly temporary closure begins to look like a vehicle for an irreversible act.

item.title: Judge corners Trump DOJ over changing story on golf course renovation
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: The Justice Department’s defense of closing East Potomac Park unraveled in court Friday when its own lawyer acknowledged that the government acted after President Donald Trump directed it to take over the golf course—not because an Oct. 9 National Park Service assessment had declared the entire park an imminent danger. item.content:encoded:
The Justice Department’s defense of closing East Potomac Park unraveled in court Friday when its own lawyer acknowledged that the government acted after President Donald Trump directed it to take over the golf course—not because an Oct. 9 National Park Service assessment had declared the entire park an imminent danger. The admission mattered because Justice Department attorneys had tried to justify the shutdown with a far more alarming story: a deteriorating seawall posed such a grave hazard that children could die.

Judge Ana Reyes exposed the contradiction by forcing the government to account for its documents, its chronology and the roughly 30,000 people allowed onto the island for the Marine Corps Marathon shortly before officials characterized the site as an emergency.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

An emergency that appeared after the directive

According to Lawfare’s Molly Roberts, who reported the hearing on Bluesky, Justice Department lawyers Stanley Woodward and Adam R.F. Gustafson argued that conditions around the island required its complete closure. Gustafson distinguished the marathon from ordinary park use by saying that “a well-organized race in broad daylight doesn’t present the same risk as children walking in the dark along the deteriorating seawall.”

The courtroom laughed. East Potomac Park closes at night: a gate blocks access to its parking lot at dusk. More importantly, the government still had to explain why risks near portions of the seawall required shutting down the whole island, particularly when earlier statements indicated that hazardous areas would be fenced off.

Reyes repeatedly asked Gustafson to identify where acting National Park Service Director Jessica Bowron’s Oct. 9 declaration said conditions endangered life and limb or warranted closing the entire park. Gustafson read technical descriptions of deteriorating mortar and a sidewalk that floods with the tides twice daily. Those details described maintenance problems. They did not supply the warning the Justice Department had attributed to the declaration.

After trying and failing to locate such language, Gustafson conceded: “I’m sorry, my mistake.” He then said the declaration had been filed “well before the decision to close the park.”

That retreat created another problem.

The president’s order, finally acknowledged

Reyes pointed to Trump’s posts on Oct. 18 and 19 saying he had issued a directive. By Oct. 30, the government said it was carrying that directive out.

“You’re carrying out the president’s directive, right?” she asked.

“And that’s the way government works,” the Justice Department replied.

The statement was less a legal explanation than an admission about the chain of command. Trump made the decision; executive agencies implemented it; Justice Department lawyers supplied the courtroom defense. Reyes noted that she had made essentially that point for hours during an earlier hearing, only to have the government insist she was wrong.

“But I guess I wasn’t,” she said.

The exchange stripped away the administration’s misdirection. The operative source of power was not a newly discovered engineering condition independently forcing park officials’ hands. It was a presidential directive connected to Trump’s plans for the golf course. Safety concerns may be real—the seawall is deteriorating, and the government says it is spending $300 million to repair it—but the existence of a repair problem does not establish that an immediate, island-wide closure was necessary.

A long-known problem becomes suddenly urgent

A second National Park Service declaration, filed Oct. 28, described the seawall as dangerous and falling apart. Reyes asked what had changed since Oct. 9, when the earlier declaration did not characterize the entire park as an urgent threat.

The deterioration was not a surprise. Reyes said the Park Service had known about the issue since 2011 and that assessments had been conducted beginning in 2019. Yet officials permitted the Marine Corps Marathon to bring more than 30,000 people along Ohio Drive near the end of October without previously announcing that the seawall posed an emergency requiring the island’s closure.

“Suddenly, on Oct. 28, days after 30k+ people ran around Ohio Drive, it’s an emergent situation,” Reyes observed.

The Justice Department invoked limited resources and agency discretion. That explanation did not persuade the judge, who contrasted it with the government’s $300 million seawall repair project. Nor did it resolve the shifting chronology: an Oct. 9 filing without the claimed emergency, Trump’s Oct. 18 and 19 statements about his directive, and an Oct. 28 declaration presenting the condition as newly urgent.

The seawall can be hazardous and the government’s account can still be evasive. Reyes was not required to deny the physical deterioration to examine whether officials elevated it into a rationale for a closure ordered for another reason.

Her closing quip captured the credibility problem the Justice Department created for itself: “I’m just trying to figure out which iteration of me not paying attention to the president I’m supposed to go with today.”

The administration’s lawyers ultimately confirmed the fact they had resisted: the president’s directive drove government action. Their safety argument did not erase that decision. It merely obscured who made it.

item.title: Trump’s DOJ makes 'wild' claims about illegal voters born in the future
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: The Justice Department’s supposed evidence of illegal voting included people who were not registered in the counties where the government placed them, naturalized citizens, duplicate records and birth dates as late as 2044. The Trump administration used those defective lists to support an extraordinary pre-midterm claim: that hundreds of thousands of noncitizens might be registered to vote. item.content:encoded:
The Justice Department’s supposed evidence of illegal voting included people who were not registered in the counties where the government placed them, naturalized citizens, duplicate records and birth dates as late as 2044. The Trump administration used those defective lists to support an extraordinary pre-midterm claim: that hundreds of thousands of noncitizens might be registered to vote. When California officials and outside experts examined the data, the allegation shrank into a demonstration of how federal power can manufacture suspicion from bad records.

Santa Cruz finds voters from nowhere—and the future

In Santa Cruz County, top election official Tricia Webber received a Justice Department list naming 81 suspected noncitizens purportedly registered there. More than half were not registered in the county, she told NPR. Some names matched neither current nor former registrants. Other entries carried dates of birth “well into the future,” including 2044.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Those were not minor clerical defects in an otherwise sound finding. They undermined the government’s basic claim that the listed people were identifiable voters, registered in the stated jurisdiction and plausibly ineligible because of their citizenship status.

Other California counties reported similarly obvious problems, including duplicate entries. Even Justice Department attorneys acknowledged under questioning from judges that the lists were flawed.

A quarter-million claim becomes a “ceiling”

Before the midterms, President Donald Trump claimed that 250,000 noncitizens were registered across four states, including California. After state officials challenged that assertion, administration officials retreated to describing the number as a “ceiling” of possible noncitizen registrants.

That change matters. A claim that 250,000 noncitizens are registered presents a purported fact. Calling the same number a theoretical upper boundary concedes that the administration did not know whether those people existed as described. The large number still performed its political function: it placed election officials on the defensive and cast lawful voter rolls as presumptively contaminated.

Federal officials escalated the allegation in mid-October by sending California a list of 20,000 people they characterized as “likely” noncitizens on the state’s voter roll. After a federal judge permitted University of California data experts to examine it during the final days before the midterms, their analysis found that 42 percent of the names did not appear on California’s current voter roll. The list also included naturalized citizens, who are eligible to vote.

The administration’s framing directed suspicion downward, toward voters, while the documented failures ran upward through the federal agencies that assembled and promoted the data. Naturalized Americans were made to carry the insinuation of fraud because the government’s methodology could not reliably distinguish citizenship from noncitizenship—or even current voters from people absent from the roll.

The lawsuit disappears before the reckoning

U.S. District Judge David Carter had planned proceedings to evaluate the accuracy of the Justice Department’s lists in the federal government’s lawsuit against California. That examination will not occur because the department dropped the case.

Dropping the lawsuit ended the immediate judicial route to testing evidence the administration had already deployed publicly. It did not answer how the lists were produced, why obvious defects survived federal review or how uncertain matches became accusations against identifiable groups of voters.

Loyola Law School professor Justin Levitt said another question remains: whether federal officials violated the Privacy Act by using California voter-roll data to generate the lists without following required public-notice procedures. That is an unresolved legal question, not an established violation. But it points to the institutional issue the inflated numbers obscured. The government was not merely making loose campaign rhetoric; federal agencies were handling voter data and generating suspicion lists under the authority of the state.

David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, said an incoming Democratic congressional majority could investigate how the administration assembled the material. He predicted “very serious scrutiny” of the Department of Homeland Security and its methodology in what he called a failed attempt to demonstrate widespread noncitizen voting.

The central result is already plain from the reporting: the administration alleged a vast electoral problem, produced lists that included lawful citizens and impossible birthdays, conceded flaws in court, and then withdrew the case before a judge could assess the evidence. The people born in 2044 were never the scandal. The scandal was that the Justice Department treated data that absurd as a usable instrument of federal accusation.

item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: A federal judge confronted the Trump administration on Friday over shifting explanations for closing a public golf course and allegations that officials destroyed related records despite a court order. When a Justice Department lawyer tried to justify Donald Trump’s plans for the East Potomac Golf Links by invoking his electoral mandate and real-estate résumé, U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes exposed the argument’s basic defect: voters did not elect Trump to redesign a District of Columbia park. item.content:encoded:
A federal judge confronted the Trump administration on Friday over shifting explanations for closing a public golf course and allegations that officials destroyed related records despite a court order. When a Justice Department lawyer tried to justify Donald Trump’s plans for the East Potomac Golf Links by invoking his electoral mandate and real-estate résumé, U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes exposed the argument’s basic defect: voters did not elect Trump to redesign a District of Columbia park.

The exchange mattered beyond the embarrassment of a government attorney. The administration was asking a court to treat presidential preference as public authorization while questions remained about compliance with an injunction and the preservation of records sought for future congressional scrutiny.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

An electoral mandate does not convey a city park

Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General Adam R.F. Gustafson argued that voters chose Trump because “he’s a builder,” according to Lawfare senior editor Molly Roberts. Reyes responded: “People elected him so he could do golf courses in the District?”

Gustafson repeated that voters knew Trump’s experience as a builder and his success in real estate. Appellate attorney Gabriel Malor, observing the hearing, called the argument “very cringe.”

The problem was not merely clumsy advocacy. Gustafson converted a national election into purported consent for one specific development project—a plan to transform East Potomac Golf Links and the surrounding park into what Trump has described as a “World Class, championship-level golf course.” Local groups have sued to stop it.

That theory erases every institution between a president and a public asset: courts, local residents, preservation requirements and the limits of executive authority. Winning an election grants defined governmental powers. It does not make the president’s personal development instincts legally controlling.

The rationale changed after the court intervened

Reyes also pressed the administration on its evolving account of why the park needed to close. Trump initially presented the closure as necessary for renovations, according to the courtroom reporting. After Reyes blocked that plan, the administration invoked safety concerns.

Under questioning, Gustafson conceded that renovation remained one rationale. Reyes then pointed to Trump’s own conduct: he had visited the course during the summer, yet apparently had not demanded immediate action to address any danger to people.

“If he had seen safety concerns to human individuals, wouldn’t he have insisted that something get done immediately?” she asked.

Court reporter Chris Geidner described Reyes’s questioning as a series with “only one answer” unfavorable to Gustafson, who was “squirming.” The substantive issue beneath that discomfort was whether the administration had repackaged a blocked renovation project as an urgent safety measure. The hearing did not resolve that question, but the government’s admission prevented it from cleanly separating the asserted hazard from Trump’s development ambitions.

Records are now part of the fight

The hearing also arose amid whistleblower allegations that administration officials were destroying documents connected to Trump’s D.C. projects in anticipation of investigations by an incoming Democratic congressional majority. Those remain allegations, but Reyes made clear that substantiated destruction would bring immediate consequences.

“If I find credible evidence of any document destruction, I will start proceedings on sanctions or contempt within a zeptosecond,” she said.

The Independent reported that Democrats had demanded that officials preserve existing record collections and productions, recover deleted material and suspend destruction practices. That demand identifies where the institutional stakes now sit: an administration facing prospective oversight controls the records that investigators would need to reconstruct its decisions.

Document preservation is not clerical housekeeping in that setting. It determines whether Congress and the courts can test official explanations against the government’s own internal record. If relevant material was destroyed, the damage would extend beyond this golf-course dispute to the ability of other branches to impose accountability at all.

The public was present, even if the argument excluded it

Gustafson also resisted acknowledging opposition to the design after Reyes told him that people in Washington were “very upset” about it. The judge then asked those in the courtroom who opposed the project to raise their hands.

More than 100 people were present, according to the account, and Reyes said the “vast majority” raised their hands. She instructed Gustafson to turn around and look.

A courtroom show of hands is not a legal finding or a scientific measure of citywide opinion. It did, however, puncture the government’s rhetorical maneuver. The administration’s lawyer had invoked an abstract national electorate to justify Trump’s preferred use of a local public space while declining to confront the residents physically assembled behind him.

That is the misdirection at the center of the case: presidential power presented as popular will, a renovation repackaged as safety, and a contested vanity project treated as though election victory settled every subsequent question. Reyes’s warning placed the actual unresolved issue back where it belongs—not on Trump’s brand as a builder, but on whether his administration obeyed the court and preserved the evidence needed to find out.
